issues.legal_issue: A plaint may be amended to enhance an alternative damages claim where the amendment concerns relief based on facts already pleaded, the trial has not commenced, and the opposing party can meet the amended claim without irreparable prejudice.
material_facts: The pending suit sought specific performance and, in the alternative, damages; the original plaint already pleaded a claim for damages.
The plaintiffs sought to increase the damages claimed, relying on the increase in the value of the property and the delay in prosecuting the suit.
The trial had not commenced, and the defendant was permitted to file an additional written statement and contest the amended claim.
The courts below left the limitation issue open for determination at trial.
issues.conclusion: The amendment was properly allowed, and the order allowing it was upheld; the appeal was dismissed, with limitation left open for trial.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 CPC, amendments necessary to determine the real controversy should generally be allowed where they do not introduce an entirely new cause of action, cause injustice that cannot be compensated by costs, withdraw an admission conferring a right on the other side, or defeat an accrued legal right. Limitation is a relevant discretionary consideration, but an amendment is not automatically barred merely because a fresh claim might be time-barred; where limitation is a disputed issue, it may be left for trial. The Court relied on L.J. Leach & Co. Ltd. v. Jardine Skinner & Co., Charan Das v. Amir Khan, Pirgonda Hongonda Patil v. Kalgonda Shidgonda Patil, Ganga Bai v. Vijay Kumar, Ganesh Trading Co. v. Moji Ram, South Konkan Distilleries v. Prabhakar Gajanan Naik, A.K. Gupta & Sons Ltd. v. Damodar Valley Corporation, Pankaja v. Yellappa, Ragu Thilak D. John v. S. Rayappan, Vishwambhar v. Laxminarayan, Vineet Kumar v. Mangal Sain Wadhera, and B.K. Narayana Pillai v. Parameswaran Pillai.

rule.if: pending_specific_performance_suit and damages_already_claimed and amendment_only_enhances_relief_on_pleaded_facts and trial_not_commenced and opposing_party_can_contest_amendment and not irreparable_prejudice

predicates.pending_specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff has a pending suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.damages_already_claimed: The plaintiff's existing pleading already seeks damages in the alternative.
predicates.amendment_only_enhances_relief_on_pleade: The proposed change increases or adjusts the relief sought on facts already set out in the pleading, rather than introducing an entirely new case.
predicates.trial_not_commenced: The trial has not begun when the amendment is sought.
predicates.opposing_party_can_contest_amendment: The opposing party can respond to the amendment and challenge the claim in the proceedings.
predicates.irreparable_prejudice: The amendment would cause the opposing party prejudice that cannot be remedied, including by costs or an opportunity to respond.

issues.definition: When an amendment in a pending specific-performance suit increases an existing damages claim on pleaded facts before trial, and the other side can contest it without irreparable prejudice, the amendment is allowed.

issues.legal_issue: The bar against omitting a claim or relief in an earlier suit does not apply to an application to amend the pleading in the same pending suit.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought to amend the plaint in the existing suit, which had not yet been adjudicated.
The defendant argued that the claim for increased damages was barred because of the omission or relinquishment contemplated by Order II Rule 2 CPC.
issues.conclusion: Order II Rule 2 CPC did not bar the amendment application because the plaintiffs sought amendment in the existing suit rather than bringing a subsequent suit.
issues.legal_principle: Order II Rule 2 CPC bars a subsequent suit in specified circumstances, including where a plaintiff omits a relief arising from the same cause of action without leave. A plea under the rule requires proof of the identity of the cause of action and the other statutory conditions; it does not govern amendment of pleadings in the one pending suit. The Court relied on Mohd. Khalil Khan v. Mahbub Ali Mian, Gurbux Singh v. Bhooralal, Upendra Narain Roy v. Rai Janoki Nath Roy, and Vaish Cooperative Adarsh Bank Ltd. v. Geetanjali Despande.

predicates.claim_amendment_in_pending_suit: A party seeks to add or alter a claim by amending the pleading in a suit that is still pending.
predicates.subsequent_suit: The party brings a new suit after the earlier suit.

issues.definition: If a party seeks to change a claim within the pending suit rather than bring a later suit, the bar applicable to certain subsequent suits does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: Constructive res judicata does not bar an amendment application that has not already been finally adjudicated after a full hearing.
material_facts: The challenged amendment was sought in the pending suit and concerned an increase in the alternative damages claim.
The litigation before the Court concerned interlocutory orders allowing the amendment, rather than a final adjudication of the amended claim after a full hearing.
issues.conclusion: The principle of constructive res judicata did not apply to the amendment application.
issues.legal_principle: Constructive res judicata does not apply in the circumstances identified by the Court where there has been no formal adjudication between the parties after a full hearing; the amendment request arose while the underlying claim remained pending.

predicates.amendment_sought_in_pending_proceeding: A party seeks an amendment while the underlying proceeding remains pending.
predicates.no_final_adjudication_after_full_hearing: The issue raised by the amendment has not been formally and finally decided between the parties after a full hearing.

issues.definition: When an amendment is sought in a pending proceeding and the issue has not been finally adjudicated after a full hearing, constructive res judicata does not bar the amendment.

issues.legal_issue: A prior ruling refusing to add an assignee as a party does not determine a later application to enhance an existing damages claim when the applications raise materially different issues and circumstances.
material_facts: The earlier proceeding concerned an assignee's application to be added as a plaintiff many years after the suit began, without an adequate explanation for the delay, and the Court found that allowing it would cause serious prejudice to the defendant.
The present application concerned increasing the amount of damages already claimed in the suit, before trial, with the limitation issue left open and an opportunity for the defendant to respond.
The earlier ruling itself recognized that delay alone is not a ground for rejecting an amendment.
issues.conclusion: The earlier decision between the parties did not govern the present amendment application and did not provide a basis for setting aside the order allowing it.
issues.legal_principle: The effect of an earlier ruling depends on the issue and circumstances it decided. A decision refusing impleadment of an assignee under Order XXII Rule 10 CPC, based on unreasonable delay and serious prejudice, does not automatically determine a different application to amend an existing claim for damages. The Court considered the earlier decision in Life Insurance Corporation of India v. Sanjeev Builders Pvt. Ltd. and the impleadment principles summarized in Vidur Impex and Traders (P) Ltd. v. Tosh Apartments (P) Ltd.

predicates.current_proceeding_seeks_to_enhance_exis: The current application seeks to increase relief already claimed in the pleading.
predicates.earlier_ruling_concerned_late_assignee_i: The earlier ruling decided whether a person claiming through an assignment could be added as a party after a substantial delay.
predicates.materially_different_application_circums: The earlier and current applications differ in the relief sought and in the circumstances relevant to prejudice and delay.

issues.definition: An earlier decision about adding a delayed assignee does not control a materially different application to enhance an existing claim.

issues.legal_issue: The provisions permitting claims for compensation in specific-performance suits do not prevent amendment under the general pleading-amendment power when the plaintiff already claimed compensation and seeks to increase it.
material_facts: The original plaint sought compensation in addition to specific performance, and the amendment sought to increase the amount of that existing claim.
The increase was based on the alleged effect of the passage of time and the change in the value of the property.
The suit remained pending, and the plaintiffs sought leave to amend rather than seeking an award of compensation without pleading it.
issues.conclusion: Section 21 of the Specific Relief Act was not strictly attracted because compensation had already been claimed; the plaintiff could seek the enhancement under Order VI Rule 17 CPC, and the provisions of the Specific Relief Act did not bar the amendment.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 21(5) and 22(2) of the Specific Relief Act require a claim for the relevant compensation or other relief to be included in the pleading, and their provisos permit amendment at any stage to add an omitted claim. Those provisions do not exclude the court's separate power under Order VI Rule 17 CPC to allow amendment of a relief already pleaded. The Court relied on Jagdish Singh v. Natthu Singh, Shamsu Suhara Beevi v. G. Alex, Babu Lal v. Hazari Lal, and the reasoning in Kahini Developers Pvt. Ltd. v. Mukesh Morarjipanchamatia.

predicates.pending_specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff has a pending suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.compensation_already_claimed: The existing pleading already includes a claim for compensation.
predicates.amendment_seeks_to_enhance_compensation_: The proposed amendment increases the compensation sought without converting the suit into a different claim for damages.

issues.definition: In a pending specific-performance suit, a plaintiff who already pleaded compensation may seek to increase that claim using the general power to amend pleadings.
